questions.q: Why place a provider abstraction layer between your notification service and APNs, FCM, or SMS vendors?
options: It encrypts notification payloads uniformly across every channel
It merges all channels into one shared delivery queue so cross-channel ordering is preserved
It decouples core logic from third-party APIs, enabling failover and swaps
It guarantees exactly-once delivery across all downstream providers
questions.explanation: A common interface hides vendor-specific APIs, so you can fail over or replace a provider without touching core logic. It cannot add exactly-once semantics providers do not offer.

questions.q: What role does a message queue play between the notification service and channel workers?
options: It absorbs bursts and decouples senders from slow third-party providers
It ranks pending notifications by predicted user engagement
It serves as the durable long-term system of record for registered device tokens
It converts payloads between the different channel formats
questions.explanation: The queue buffers traffic spikes and lets workers drain at provider-safe rates, so a slow vendor never blocks the request path. Token storage belongs in a database, not a queue.

questions.q: What exactly is a push device token?
options: The user's hashed account identifier shared across devices
A platform-issued handle addressing one app install on one device
A session cookie that gets refreshed on every app launch
The device's hardware serial number registered with the OS vendor at activation time
questions.explanation: APNs or FCM issues the token to a specific app installation on a specific device, so one user with several devices or reinstalls has several distinct tokens.

questions.q: Which channel's strict per-message cost makes deduplication and throttling most financially important?
options: In-app inbox
Web push
Email
SMS texts
questions.explanation: SMS is billed per message by carriers, often at cents each, so duplicates directly burn money. Push and in-app messages are essentially free per send.

questions.q: What does a quiet hours feature do in a notification system?
options: Blocks every notification permanently for users who opted out
Defers non-urgent notifications during the user's configured local-time window
Batches all notifications into a single weekly digest email
Mutes only the channels showing low engagement scores
questions.explanation: Quiet hours holds low-priority sends until the user's local window ends, rather than dropping them. Urgent classes like security alerts typically bypass the window.

questions.q: Where should user notification preferences be enforced?
options: Server-side in the pipeline before enqueueing to channel workers
On the device after delivery, by hiding the unwanted notifications
At the provider, using per-token filtering rules they maintain
In the analytics pipeline once sends have been recorded
questions.explanation: Filtering before enqueue avoids paying for and transmitting unwanted messages, and works uniformly across all clients. Client-side hiding still sends and still costs money.

questions.q: What is a dead-letter queue used for in a notification pipeline?
options: Storing notifications addressed to deleted user accounts
Ordering pending retries according to their priority class before redelivery
Holding messages that failed all retries for later inspection or replay
Archiving successfully delivered notifications for audits
questions.explanation: A DLQ parks messages that exhausted their retries so they stop blocking the main queue, while preserving them for debugging or manual replay after a fix.

questions.q: What does notification collapsing mean?
options: Compressing each notification payload's bytes before handing it off to the providers
Silently dropping any notification older than one hour
Merging the queues of multiple channels into a single stream
Replacing several related pending notifications with a single summary
questions.explanation: Collapsing uses a key so newer messages supersede older undelivered ones, showing '5 new messages' instead of five alerts. It is about display, not byte compression.

questions.q: FCM responds that a device token is unregistered. What should your system do?
options: Remove the token from the registry so future sends skip it
Retry with exponential backoff until the token re-registers itself
Fall back to delivering that notification over SMS instead
Rotate the server's API credentials and resend the message
questions.explanation: Unregistered is a permanent error meaning the app was uninstalled or the token replaced, so pruning it keeps the registry clean. Retrying only wastes quota and never succeeds.

questions.q: A send request to a provider times out and your worker immediately retries. What risk does this create?
options: Token expiry, since repeated retries invalidate device tokens
Duplicate notifications, because the timed-out attempt may have actually succeeded
A deadlock between the retry topic and the main delivery topic
A provider ban for exceeding the allowed concurrent connections
questions.explanation: A timeout is ambiguous: the provider may have accepted and delivered the message before the response was lost, so a blind retry can double-notify the user.

questions.q: The same business event triggers notification requests from two producer services. What is the standard guard against double-sending?
options: Serialize both producers through a single queue partition so events arrive in a strict order
Let the client suppress alerts that look visually identical
Hash the payload bytes and have the provider drop equal hashes
An event-derived dedupe key checked against a recent-delivery store before send
questions.explanation: A deterministic idempotency key derived from the event id lets a fast store like Redis reject the second request. Ordering alone does not stop two distinct sends.

questions.q: How should per-user notification frequency capping be implemented?
options: Through the provider's built-in API quotas applied at the sending account level
In the client app, by hiding alerts beyond a daily threshold
Per-user caps in the pipeline, with overrides for critical classes
By slowing overall queue consumption whenever volume spikes
questions.explanation: Caps must be tracked per recipient server-side to limit fatigue, with exemptions so security codes and other critical alerts always get through. Account-level quotas are not per user.

questions.q: During a large marketing blast, how do you keep OTP delivery latency low?
options: Separate priority queues so transactional sends never wait behind bulk campaigns
Send OTPs exclusively over SMS, which delivers faster than push
Temporarily increase worker count across the whole pipeline
Tag OTP messages with a higher-priority collapse key
questions.explanation: Isolating transactional traffic in its own queue with dedicated workers prevents head-of-line blocking behind millions of bulk messages. Adding workers alone still drains one shared backlog.

questions.q: Your email provider reports a hard bounce for an address. What is the correct handling?
options: Schedule weekly retries with backoff in case the mailbox comes back online
Move the user to a different email provider and resend
Ignore it, since bounce management is provider-internal
Add the address to a suppression list to protect sender reputation
questions.explanation: A hard bounce means the address is permanently invalid; continuing to mail it raises your bounce rate and can get your domain blocklisted, so suppress it immediately.

questions.q: Where should message templates and localization be applied?
options: In each producing service, embedding final text into the event
In the notification service at send time, using the user's locale and channel template
On the device, which ships with every template preinstalled
At the provider, which localizes payloads automatically
questions.explanation: Rendering centrally at send time keeps events as structured data and lets copy, locale, and per-channel formatting change without redeploying every producer.

questions.q: How should a broadcast notification to 50 million users be dispatched?
options: One multicast API call carrying all fifty million device tokens
A synchronous loop inside the API request that triggered the broadcast
A batch job streams user segments into queues with rate control against provider limits
Devices hold persistent server connections and receive one broadcast frame
questions.explanation: Fanning out asynchronously in chunks lets you respect provider batch sizes and rate limits, checkpoint progress, and resume after failures. Providers cap multicast at a few hundred tokens per call.

questions.q: A push provider degrades and aggressive retries from your workers deepen the outage. What is the right defense?
options: Reroute all pending traffic into the dead-letter queue until the provider fully recovers
Raise the per-message retry count so everything eventually lands
Switch workers to synchronous sends to preserve strict ordering
Backoff with jitter plus a circuit breaker that pauses sends to the sick provider
questions.explanation: Jittered backoff spreads retries apart and the breaker stops hammering a failing dependency, letting it recover. More retries would only amplify the retry storm.

questions.q: After a long outage you replay the dead-letter queue. What risk must be handled first?
options: Replayed messages may be stale; enforce per-message TTLs and drop expired ones
Replay reorders the queues; re-sort every message by its original enqueue timestamp
Replay double-counts delivery analytics; recompute metrics afterward
Replay may overload the DLQ itself; shard it before starting
questions.explanation: Time-sensitive content like expired OTPs or finished flash sales is worse than useless hours later, so a TTL check should discard obsolete messages before replay.

questions.q: A user reinstalls the app, and pushes sent to the old token silently vanish. What practice prevents this?
options: Nothing is needed, since tokens never change for a given device
Re-register on each app start and retire older tokens recorded for that device
Providers automatically forward old-token sends to the new install
Encrypt device tokens so that stale copies fail decryption and get purged automatically
questions.explanation: Refreshing the token at launch and unmapping superseded tokens for the same device or user keeps the registry current. Tokens do change on reinstall, OS updates, and restores.

questions.q: A notification pipeline advertises exactly-once delivery to devices. Why is that claim unsound?
options: Queues cannot persist messages durably enough to support exactly-once
Device tokens rotate too frequently for acknowledgments to bind
End-to-end acks across providers and devices are not transactional, so at-least-once plus dedupe is the practical bound
Exactly-once requires synchronized clocks, which mobile devices lack
questions.explanation: You cannot atomically commit a send with a third-party provider and an offline device, so ambiguous outcomes are unavoidable. The realistic design is at-least-once with idempotent dedupe.
